The Mongol conquests were the wars in which the Mongols, a nomad people of the eastern steppe, built the largest land empire in history in the thirteenth century, from Korea to Hungary. The chart shows them from 1206, when Temüjin became Genghis Khan, to the death of his grandson Kublai in 1294.

Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes and turned them into a disciplined army of mounted archers, organised in units of ten, a hundred and a thousand. He attacked northern China, and from 1219 invaded the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia and Iran, destroying great cities such as Merv and Nishapur.

His sons and grandsons carried on, building the Mongol Empire:

  • They finished off northern China's Jin dynasty in 1234.
  • Batu and Subutai conquered the Rus principalities and in 1241 invaded Poland and Hungary. They pulled back when the great khan died.
  • Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258 and ended the Abbasid caliphate. The Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260.
  • Kublai Khan conquered southern China, founding the Yuan dynasty. His fleets against Japan and Java failed.

After 1260 the empire split into four khanates: the Golden Horde in Russia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, the Ilkhanate in Iran and the Yuan in China.

The conquests were devastating. Millions died, and some regions took centuries to recover. Yet Mongol rule also made it safe to cross Asia for a time. Merchants, envoys and missionaries travelled from Europe to China, ideas and goods moved, and so, it seems, did the plague that became the Black Death.
